fields.description_1:
AC Drive needs to help learner drivers choose a lesson route before they understand differences between packages, exam preparation and requirements. A driving-school site can easily become a price list, but price alone does not explain what a learner is selecting or what the next step involves. The information needed clearer order around the decision.

The website therefore had to introduce lesson choices first, then connect package and practical details to those choices before booking or contact. On mobile, comparison and actions needed to remain easy to scan. The portfolio story also had to avoid promises about pass rates, lesson counts or learning speed. The challenge was to make AC Drive straightforward for new learners without turning a learning process into a guaranteed package outcome.
fields.description_2:
I organised AC Drive around the choices a learner makes before booking. Lesson routes provide the starting point, followed by package information and practical details that belong to each option. Exam-related information supports the decision without taking over the first screen, and booking or contact appears once the visitor has enough context to continue.

I kept labels direct so new drivers do not need specialist driving-school language to understand the offer. On smaller screens, lesson cards, package details and actions keep a predictable sequence. The portfolio text avoids claiming that a package guarantees a fixed number of lessons or exam success. It now explains how WordPress supports a clear route from lesson comparison to a useful next step while keeping educational outcomes appropriately individual.

fields.description_1:
Image Usage Scanner solves a WordPress maintenance question that is deceptively difficult: where is a media item being used? Images can appear as featured media, in normal content or inside supported ACF fields, so deleting or replacing a file based on one screen can break references elsewhere. The tool needed to gather evidence without changing the content it inspects.

Large libraries also create operational problems because scans can be interrupted by browser refreshes, timeouts or overlapping workers. Results therefore needed resumable processing, safe locking and exportable reporting. The portfolio story had to make the read-only boundary explicit and avoid promising automatic cleanup. The challenge was to turn scattered media relationships into reviewable information while keeping the scan safe enough to run on real WordPress installations.
fields.description_2:
I built Image Usage Scanner as an admin-only audit workflow that reports media relationships instead of modifying them. It checks featured images and supported ACF image or gallery fields in bounded batches, saving progress so a scan can continue after interruption. Short locks prevent overlapping work, while stale-lock recovery handles abandoned processing safely.

Terminal states are protected from older workers, and the interface can resume polling after a refresh. Findings can be exported to CSV with protection against spreadsheet formula injection. Capability checks, nonces and validated scan identifiers keep the workflow inside the admin boundary. The portfolio case now explains the plugin as evidence for later cleanup decisions, not as an automatic deletion tool or a promise that every possible media reference can be discovered.

fields.description_1:
Course Dates Manager addresses a publishing problem that appears when course information and dates are maintained in pages. Editors can end up repeating programme details, schedules and category information in several places, which makes updates harder to keep consistent. The project needed a structured WordPress model rather than another collection of manually formatted course blocks.

That structure also had to support a public overview and controlled external access without exposing unpublished content or loading unnecessary assets everywhere. Queries needed sensible limits, and the frontend had to remain usable on smaller screens. The portfolio story had to focus on the real content-management problem rather than generic education marketing. The challenge was to connect editor-friendly course management with a reusable public presentation and a bounded API surface.
fields.description_2:
I built Course Dates Manager around a dedicated course post type and taxonomy so programme information can be maintained in one structured place. A responsive shortcode renders the public overview, while paginated REST endpoints expose only published course data for integrations that need it. This separates the content model from the presentation without duplicating the source.

The frontend uses lightweight JavaScript and accessible accordion behaviour, and assets load only where they are needed. Settings are sanitized, queries are bounded and lifecycle handling stays conservative. I kept the portfolio explanation focused on architecture and editorial workflow rather than claiming registration or learning improvements. The case now shows how WordPress can manage repeatable course information cleanly while keeping public output, API access and maintenance boundaries understandable.

fields.description_1:
AI Patch Runner deals with a high-risk WordPress task: applying structured code changes to installed plugins without turning the admin area into an unrestricted file editor. A bad patch can break functionality, so speed is less important than knowing what changes, who applies it and how to recover if the result is wrong.

The workflow therefore needed preview, apply and rollback as distinct stages, with production application disabled unless trusted server configuration and an explicit admin setting allow it. Multisite adds another permission boundary. The portfolio story also had to avoid implying that automation makes production changes inherently safe. The challenge was to make patch execution reviewable and reversible while keeping strong limits around permissions, environment and the type of change the plugin can perform.
fields.description_2:
I built AI Patch Runner as an admin-only workflow for structured JSON patch packages. Preview is kept separate from execution so a proposed change can be inspected before plugin files are modified. Production application is disabled by default and only becomes available when both trusted server configuration and the matching admin setting permit it.

Plugin-update capabilities protect normal use, while multisite requires super-admin access. Rollback belongs to the same workflow so recovery is planned before a write, not added afterward. The plugin is intentionally limited to controlled patch packages rather than arbitrary code generation or remote execution. The portfolio case now explains that safety model directly and does not claim that automation removes the need for staging, backups, technical review or environment-specific testing.

fields.description_1:
ACF CSV Manager began as a way to make structured WordPress content easier to review outside separate editing screens. Exporting ACF-oriented data to CSV can help with bulk review, but importing changes back creates risk when rows, fields or content ownership are unclear. A controlled process was needed so convenience did not turn into uncontrolled bulk edits.

The project later overlapped with ACF Page Text Manager, creating a maintenance problem: two similar repositories could receive duplicate fixes and drift apart. The portfolio story therefore needed to explain both the original CSV workflow and the decision to retire the duplicate. It should not present this repository as the current canonical product. The challenge was content-review efficiency first, followed by clear consolidation and ownership for future maintenance.
fields.description_2:
I developed ACF CSV Manager as an earlier workflow for exporting ACF-related content into a reviewable spreadsheet format and returning approved updates through WordPress. The design demonstrated how bulk text work could be organised without opening every page individually, while keeping the import process separate from normal editing.

As the feature set converged with ACF Page Text Manager, I stopped treating both repositories as active products. Development was consolidated into the canonical ACF-Text-Manager repository, while the older code remains useful for history and rollback reference. Migration guidance points toward the maintained version instead of encouraging duplicate releases. The portfolio case now describes both stages accurately: the original structured CSV problem and the later engineering decision to reduce duplication and make ownership clearer.
